screens.title: What is Raycasting?
screens.narratorSegment: Raycasting is a one-shot physics query where we imagine firing an invisible line, or ray, from a point in a direction and asking what it intersects. Think of it as a laser pointer you can test in a single frame. The method is synchronous: it returns a boolean telling you if something was hit and optionally fills a RaycastHit structure with rich details about the impact. Raycasts are ideal when you need an immediate answer—what is the player pointing at right now, is there ground below a foot, or does an AI have line-of-sight to the player. A common misuse is relying on raycasts for continuous collision response; raycasts are queries, not replacements for physics simulation. For robust results, rays require colliders to be present on target objects. If a target has no collider the ray simply passes through. Remember that triggers can be hit by default, so decide whether you want to treat triggers as solid hits. To check correctness during development, use Debug. DrawRay to visualize the origin, direction, and length of each ray. How might you convert a single ray into a slightly thicker check if a thin geometry misses? Consider sphere or box casts as alternatives.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A raycast queries the physics scene along a line and returns whether a collider was hit plus hit details.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Raycasting?

Raycasting explained

A single, directional physics query that returns whether it intersects a collider and provides impact details.

Key properties returned
  • Impact point in world space
  • Surface normal at the hit
  • Collider and the GameObject that was hit
Concrete example
Use a camera ray to determine which object the player is looking at and then highlight that object when hit.
Common pitfall
Rays ignore objects without colliders. If a selection fails, check for a missing collider or wrong layer.
Key Takeaway

Raycasts are precise, immediate queries ideal for single-frame decisions like aiming or selection.

Analogy

Imagine shining a laser pointer: anything the beam touches is a hit. If the object is too thin you might miss, so you might widen the beam if needed.

Visual checks
  • Use Debug.DrawRay to see the exact path.
  • Log hit.point and hit.normal to inspect results.
  • Toggle layers to confirm filtering works.
Reflection
If a ray fails to hit what you expect, check colliders first, then layer assignments, then aim and distance settings.

screens.title: Physics.Raycast: Parameters and Return
screens.narratorSegment: Physics. Raycast is the central A P I for linear queries. The typical call takes an origin Vector3, a direction Vector3, an out RaycastHit to receive hit details, and a maxDistance to limit how far the ray travels. It can also accept a LayerMask and a QueryTriggerInteraction option. The method returns true if something is hit within maxDistance and false otherwise. The RaycastHit struct provides the impact point, surface normal, the collider that was hit, and the associated GameObject. Practically, you will call Physics. Raycast inside Update when you need a frame-by-frame check, for example to show an interaction prompt. But remember to keep maxDistance sensible to avoid long, expensive tests. Also prefer passing a LayerMask when possible so the physics engine only considers relevant colliders. For multi-hit scenarios use RaycastAll or a non-alloc variant that fills a preallocated array. Below is a canonical C# snippet showing the parameters and handling a hit. Read the RaycastHit fields to compute aim offsets or place effects exactly at hit. point. content.html:
API & Usage › Physics.Raycast

Typical call

Ray ray = new Ray(origin, direction);
RaycastHit hit;
if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, maxDistance, layerMask))
{
  // hit.point, hit.normal, hit.collider
}
Notes
  • Pass a LayerMask to restrict which colliders are considered.
  • maxDistance limits checks and improves performance.
  • Overloads exist that accept origin and direction directly.

RaycastHit fields

point
World position where the ray struck the surface.
normal
Surface normal useful for aligning effects or decals.
collider
The Collider component that was hit.
transform / gameObject
Use to change color, call methods, or attach effects.
Example outcome

Use hit.point to spawn an impact effect precisely where the ray struck.

screens.title: LayerMasks: Create and Use
screens.narratorSegment: LayerMasks are bitmasks that tell the physics system which layers to consider in queries. Every GameObject can be assigned to one layer. In practice you create a layer named Interactable, assign that layer to objects you want the raycast to hit, and then pass a LayerMask into Physics. Raycast. In code you can declare a public LayerMask field and set it in the Inspector, or build one with LayerMask. GetMask by name. The benefit is twofold: first, logical—your interaction code only considers relevant objects; second, performance—the physics engine avoids checking colliders on excluded layers. A common developer mistake is confusing layer numbers and masks: LayerMask values are bitfields, while Layer numbers are simple integers. When debugging, toggle layer visibility in the Inspector and verify that your ray responds only to the included layers. This small setup keeps raycasts focused and predictable, especially in crowded scenes. content.html:
Layer System › LayerMasks

Create a Layer

Open the Layers dropdown and add a user layer named Interactable. Assign objects to that layer in the Inspector.

C#: Inspector-assigned mask
Declare a public LayerMask and pick layers in the Inspector. This is the simplest and safest approach.
C# helper
LayerMask mask = LayerMask.GetMask("Interactable");

Common mistakes

  • Passing a layer number where a mask is expected. Masks are bitfields; use GetMask or a public LayerMask.
  • Forgetting to assign the GameObject's Layer in the Inspector so the mask has no effect.
  • Expecting tags to filter physics: tags are not used by Physics.Raycast directly.
Why this matters

A correct LayerMask narrows checks and prevents unintended hits like the player body or environment props.

content.html:
Practical Script › RaycastInteraction.cs
Starter Code
using UnityEngine;

public class RaycastInteraction : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float interactionDistance = 10f;
  public LayerMask interactableLayer; // Assign in Inspector
  public Color rayColor = Color.green;

  Camera cam;

  void Awake()
  {
    cam = Camera.main;
  }

  void Update()
  {
    Ray ray = cam.ScreenPointToRay(new Vector3(Screen.width/2, Screen.height/2, 0));
    RaycastHit hit;

    Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * interactionDistance, rayColor);

    if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, interactionDistance, interactableLayer))
    {
      Debug.Log($"Looking at: {hit.collider.gameObject.name}");
      Renderer r = hit.collider.GetComponent();
      if (r != null) r.material.color = Color.yellow;
    }
  }
}
Integration checklist
  • Create an Interactable layer and assign it to objects.
  • Attach the script to Main Camera and set the LayerMask in Inspector.
  • Run the scene and point at the object to observe the highlight and console log.
Extension idea
Call an Interactable interface on hit to perform context-specific actions instead of changing material directly.
Key Takeaway

Expose the LayerMask in the Inspector and cache the Camera for a robust implementation.

screens.title: Using Raycasts for Ground Checks
screens.narratorSegment: A short downward raycast is a common and reliable technique to determine whether a character is grounded. Instead of relying solely on collision callbacks, cast from slightly above the character's feet downwards using a small maxDistance equal to the expected gap. If the ray hits, use the RaycastHit. point and distance to decide whether the character can jump or should switch to a grounded movement mode. For sloped terrain, examine hit. normal to align movement and to prevent snapping issues. If the player is on thin geometry or fast-moving platforms, consider using a SphereCast for a slightly thicker detection area. Remember that the ray will not hit objects without colliders. Also pay attention to layer filtering: include the ground and moving platforms while excluding triggers or the player body. Test on slopes and staircases to ensure consistent results under the expected movement speeds. Using Raycasts for Ground Checks means a downward ray (or sphere cast) with a small maxdistance reliably detects whether a character is on the ground and provides surface normals for alignment.. In practical terms, reliable grounded state for characters and movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Ground Detection › Raycasts for grounding

Downward ray pattern

Cast a short ray from the character's feet position downward. If you hit within the expected distance, mark grounded.
Handle slopes
Use hit.normal to determine walkable angles and to project movement along the surface.
When to use SphereCast
Use a small sphere cast if feet or thin colliders are missed by a single line ray.

Checklist

  • Choose an origin slightly above feet to avoid starting inside geometry.
  • Set maxDistance to a small tolerance value so small gaps are detected.

screens.title: When to Use Raycast vs Volume Casts
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between a thin line raycast and a volume cast is a practical trade-off. Use a standard Raycast when you want a precise, single-line check such as exact aiming, selecting a specific pixel-aligned target, or measuring a precise hit point for decals. Use SphereCast or BoxCast when thin colliders or high relative motion cause misses; these casts detect objects within a volume and reduce false negatives at the cost of more computation per check. For example, a downward ray for a character foot might miss a narrow gap—SphereCast with a small radius is more forgiving and more likely to report grounded state. If you need multiple objects along the line, RaycastAll returns all hits, but it allocates memory; prefer RaycastNonAlloc with a reused array in tight loops. Always weigh the cost of extra checks against the cost of missed detections and extra code complexity. Start simple with a Raycast, then switch to a volume cast if testing reveals instability. Deciding between a thin line raycast and a volume cast is a practical trade-off. Use a standard Raycast when you want a precise, single-line check such as exact aiming, selecting a specific pixel-aligned target, or measuring a precise hit point for decals. Use SphereCast or BoxCast when thin colliders or high relative motion cause misses; these casts detect objects within a volume and reduce false negatives at the cost of more computation per check. For example, a downward ray for a character foot might miss a narrow gap—SphereCast with a small radius is more forgiving and more likely to report grounded state. If you need multiple objects along the line, RaycastAll returns all hits, but it allocates memory; prefer RaycastNonAlloc with a reused array in tight loops. Always weigh the cost of extra checks against the cost of missed detections and extra code complexity. Start simple with a Raycast, then switch to a volume cast if testing reveals instability. These are the three core ideas to take with you. First, raycasting is an immediate, directional physics query that returns whether a collider was hit and rich hit data you can use for gameplay decisions. Second, LayerMasks let you filter which objects are considered by a raycast; use them to avoid unintended hits and reduce work for the physics engine. Third, optimize by limiting maxDistance, caching references, and using non-alloc APIs or volume casts when line-based checks are unreliable. Keep Debug.
